correctness.rationale: For \(n=2^a p\), set \(A=a+1\) and \(M=2^A-1\). Cohen's Theorem 1 gives both prime-support and excess-valuation restrictions on \(\sigma(n)\). For any \(r\mid M\) with \(r\ne p\), those restrictions force \(r\mid A\), but with \(d=\operatorname{ord}_r(2)\), LTE gives \(v_r(M)=v_r(2^d-1)+v_r(A/d)>v_r(A)=v_r(\tau(n))\), a contradiction. Hence \(M=p^c\). If \(d=\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<A\) and \(m=A/d\), then \(Q=(2^A-1)/(2^d-1)\) is a pure \(p\)-power with \(v_p(Q)=v_p(m)\), so \(Q\le m\), while its geometric-sum form gives \(Q>m\); thus \(d=A\). Hence \(A\mid p-1\). An odd prime \(s\mid p+1\) would have to divide \(A\) by Cohen's support condition, and therefore \(p-1\), impossible. So \(p+1=2^u\); primality of \(p\) makes \(u\) prime and \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=u=A\), giving \(p=2^A-1\) and \(c=1\). The converse is an even perfect number. The checker confirms the defining condition for \(a\le20\) and odd primes \(p\le200000\).

value.rationale: This is a complete classification of the canonical squarefree-odd-part slice of an explicitly identified structural gap. It is not a parameter tweak: when the odd exponent is one, tau(n)=2(a+1) has exactly one nontrivial exponent factor, making this the first layer where superharmonicity might differ from harmonicity. The theorem proves that it does not, and the order/LTE mechanism isolates why.
